profile.feeling: Curiosity; also surprise and admiration.

phrases.meaning: the Four Questions of the Seder

synonyms.nuance: the classical spelling with patah, followed by a doubled consonant: מַה נִּשְׁתַּנָּה

etymology.text: Cognates such as Aramaic מָה (mā, “what”), Arabic مَا (mā, “what”) and Ugaritic 𐎎𐎅 (mh) can be found across the Central Semitic languages.

funFacts: The Passover Seder’s Four Questions open with מַה נִּשְׁתַּנָּה הַלַּיְלָה הַזֶּה — “What makes this night different?”
pitfalls: No verb “is” is needed: מָה זֶה? = What is this?
“Which …?” is usually אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ, not מָה: אֵיזֶה יָרָק? (which vegetable?).
subtleties: מָה alone (“What?!”) can express surprise or impatience, depending on the tone.

profile.feeling: Looking for things, people and places.

senses.def: where (in indirect questions: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ אֵיפֹה …)

examples.tr: I (m.) don’t know where he is.

synonyms.nuance: the formal and literary “where”
a poetic, Biblical “where (is)?”

etymology.text: From אֵי (e, “where”) + פֹּה (po, “here”).

funFacts: It is literally “where-here”: אֵי + פֹּה.
Do not confuse it with אֵיפָה “ephah” (a Biblical dry measure): אֵיפָה וְאֵיפָה (“an ephah and an ephah”) means a double standard.
pitfalls: “Where to?” is לְאָן, not אֵיפֹה: לְאָן אַתָּה הוֹלֵךְ?
Spelled with a final ה although it is pronounced efó.
subtleties: “Where are you from?” is מֵאֵיפֹה אַתָּה? (מֵ = from).

lexemes.note: Invariable: מִי הוּא? מִי הִיא? מִי הֵם? — the same word for one person or many, man or woman.

profile.feeling: Who is it? Who is coming? — the first question at the door and on the phone.

phrases.meaning: if only …, I wish (מִי יִתֵּן וְ…)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: מִי is the only “who?”.

etymology.text: Compare Ugaritic 𐎎𐎊 (my), Phoenician 𐤌𐤉 (my), El-Amarna Akkadian mīya “who”, and Levantine, Egyptian and Hijazi Arabic مين (mīn) “who” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The name מִיכָאֵל (Michael) is a question: מִי כָּאֵל — “who is like God?”.
Spoken Arabic of the Levant and Egypt says مين (mīn) for “who” — very close to מִי.
pitfalls: מִי is “who”, מָה is “what”: מִי זֶה? asks about a person, מָה זֶה? about a thing.
Unvowelled מי can also be מֵי “water(s) of” (מֵי־ before a noun) — context decides.
subtleties: It never changes: מִי הִיא? “who is she?”, מִי הֵם? “who are they?”

profile.feeling: Timetables, appointments, “when is dinner?”.

senses.def: when (in an indirect question: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ מָתַי …)

examples.text: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדַעַת מָתַי הוּא בָּא.
examples.tr: I (f.) don’t know when he is coming.

synonyms.nuance: the old, Rabbinic “when” — known from the first words of the Mishnah, מֵאֵימָתַי

etymology.text: Compare Arabic مَتَى (matā) “when” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Mishnah opens with a “when?”: מֵאֵימָתַי קוֹרִין אֶת שְׁמַע בְּעַרְבִית — “From when may one recite the Shema in the evening?” (Berakhot 1:1).
Arabic مَتَى (matā) is the same word.
pitfalls: מָתַי only asks. The “when” of a statement (“when I come …”) is כְּשֶׁ… or כַּאֲשֶׁר (lesson 18).
Unvowelled מתי can also be the name מַתִּי (Mati) — context decides.
subtleties: Stress on the last syllable: ma-TAI.

profile.feeling: How is it? How do you do it? — curiosity about manner and quality.

senses.def: how? (in what way; in what state)
how (in an indirect question: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ אֵיךְ …)

examples.tr: How do you say “thank you” in Greek?
What is your (m.) name? (“How do they call you?”)

examples.text: אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ אֵיךְ מְבַשְּׁלִים אֶת זֶה.
examples.tr: I (m.) don’t know how to cook this.

collocations.tr: what’s your name? (“how do they call you?”)

phrases.meaning: a lament over a great fall

synonyms.nuance: the formal “how” of instructions, the news and writing

etymology.text: Biblical Hebrew (אֵיךְ נָפְלוּ גִבּוֹרִים, 2 Samuel 1:19). Wiktionary gives no etymology; it begins with the question element אֵי־ of אֵיפֹה “where” and אֵיזֶה “which”.

funFacts: Greek Πώς σε λένε; Russian Как тебя зовут? and German Wie heißt du? ask the name with “how” too — exactly like אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ?
pitfalls: “What is your name?” is אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ? — with “how”, not “what” (or מָה הַשֵּׁם שֶׁלְּךָ?).
“How are you?” is not built with אֵיךְ: say מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ? or מָה נִשְׁמָע? (lesson 2).
subtleties: The final ךְ carries a shva and is said ech, one syllable.

profile.feeling: The everyday “why?” — curious, or reproachful, depending on the voice.

phrases.tr: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me
phrases.meaning: despair; the words quoted in Aramaic in the Gospels (Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani)

synonyms.nuance: the formal “why” of the news, of teachers and of official letters

etymology.text: Compare Arabic لِمَا “for what, why” (Wiktionary); built from לְ “for” + מָה “what”: “for what?”.

funFacts: The cry “Ηλί, ηλί, λαμά σαβαχθανί” of the Greek Gospels (Matthew 27:46) quotes Psalm 22 — the same לָמָה.
Wiktionary also gives the spelling לָמָה without the dot in the מ.
pitfalls: The answer “because” is כִּי in speech (מִשּׁוּם שֶׁ… in formal style) — lesson 18.
In everyday speech it is stressed on the first syllable: LA-ma.
subtleties: לָמָּה can sound like a reproach (לָמָּה לֹא?! “why not?!”); the same question with מַדּוּעַ sounds like a news report.

profile.feeling: The serious “why?” of headlines, teachers and inquiries.

examples.tr: Why are the doctors not at work?
The police officer asked why he was there.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday “why” — what friends and family say

etymology.text: Contraction of מָה “what [is]” + יָדוּעַ “known” (Wiktionary): “what is known (about it)?”.

funFacts: It is a fossil sentence: מָה יָדוּעַ “what is known?” became one word, מַדּוּעַ.
pitfalls: In conversation מַדּוּעַ sounds bookish: friends say לָמָּה.
The final ־ַעַ is a “stolen” patah, said before the ע: ma-DU-a.
subtleties: Both mean exactly “why”: the difference is only the register — like German warum (both) vs. English why / wherefore.

lexemes.note: Before the noun, agreeing with it: אֵיזֶה סֵפֶר? אֵיזוֹ כּוֹס? אֵילוּ סְפָרִים?

profile.feeling: Choosing: which one? which book, which glass?

senses.def: which? what (kind of)? — before a noun
some (any): אֵיזֶה סֵפֶר “some book or other”

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym: אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ / אֵילוּ is the only “which?”.

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives no etymology; it is the question element אֵי־ (as in אֵיפֹה “where”) + זֶה “this” (feminine אֵיזוֹ, with זוֹ).

funFacts: Greek ποιος / ποια / ποιο changes for gender just like אֵיזֶה / אֵיזוֹ.
pitfalls: It agrees with the noun: אֵיזֶה (m.), אֵיזוֹ (f.), אֵילוּ (plural). In everyday speech many people say אֵיזֶה for all — but write אֵיזוֹ before a feminine noun.
Unvowelled אילו is also אֵלּוּ “these” and אִלּוּ “if (only)” — only the vowels tell them apart.
subtleties: מָה + noun is not “which …?”: “which book?” is אֵיזֶה סֵפֶר?, never *מָה סֵפֶר?

lexemes.note: Two words, one question: שֶׁל “of” + מִי “who”.

profile.feeling: Lost and found: whose bag is this?

etymology.text: שֶׁל “of” (lesson 6) + מִי “who”: literally “of whom?”.

funFacts: German wessen, Russian чей and Greek ποιανού are single words; Hebrew builds “whose” like English “of whom”.
pitfalls: There is no one-word “whose”: always שֶׁל מִי, at the start or at the end of the question — שֶׁל מִי הַתִּיק? / הַתִּיק שֶׁל מִי?
subtleties: The answer uses the same שֶׁל: שֶׁלִּי “mine”, שֶׁל אַבָּא “Dad’s”.

profile.feeling: A white coat, a queue at the clinic — and the trusted family doctor.

examples.tr: He is a doctor in a hospital.
who heals the sick of His people Israel

synonyms.nuance: the title “Doctor” (written ד״ר before a name); as a word for the job it is informal

etymology.text: Present participle of רָפָא “to heal” (Wiktionary: the noun follows from the verb), from Proto-West Semitic *rpʔ “to heal, to protect”; compare Arabic رَفَأَ (rafaʔa) “to mend”.

funFacts: The name רְפָאֵל (Raphael) means “God heals” — the same root ר־פ־א.
To a sick person Israelis wish רְפוּאָה שְׁלֵמָה “a complete healing” — from the same root.
pitfalls: A woman doctor is רוֹפְאָה.
The final א is silent: ro-FE; with the article הָרוֹפֵא (qamats: ר never doubles).
subtleties: “To go to the doctor” takes the article, as in English: לָלֶכֶת לָרוֹפֵא.

profile.feeling: The doctor who is a woman — common in Israeli clinics and hospitals.

examples.tr: The doctor (f.) is at the hospital.
She is a very good doctor.

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the written title ד״ר is the same for women and men.

etymology.text: Feminine of רוֹפֵא “doctor”, the present participle of רָפָא “to heal” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Russian says врач for a woman too; Hebrew, like German Ärztin, always marks a woman doctor: רוֹפְאָה.
pitfalls: The plural רוֹפְאוֹת is for women only; a mixed group is רוֹפְאִים.
subtleties: Before another noun it becomes רוֹפְאַת: רוֹפְאַת יְלָדִים “a paediatrician (f.)” (Wiktionary also gives רוֹפֵאת־).

profile.feeling: Bridges, buildings and start-ups — a prestige job in Israel’s high-tech world.

examples.tr: The engineers are in the office.
My brother is a software engineer.

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym; the field is הַנְדָּסָה “engineering”.

etymology.text: From the verb הִנְדֵּס “to engineer” (Wiktionary: the noun follows from the verb), built on הַנְדָּסָה “engineering; geometry”, from Arabic هَنْدَسَة (handasa), from the Iranian source of Persian اندازه (andâze) “measuring”.

funFacts: Turkish mühendis “engineer” comes from Arabic مُهَنْدِس (muhandis) — the same word as מְהַנְדֵּס.
Arabic هَنْدَسَة and Hebrew הַנְדָּסָה mean both “engineering” and “geometry” (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: With the article the מ doubles: הַמְּהַנְדֵּס.
Stress on the last syllable: me-han-DES; plural מְהַנְדְּסִים.
subtleties: It has the shape of a piʿel present form (מְ־ … ־ֵ־), the shape of many “doers”: מְבַשֵּׁל “cooking”, מְהַנְדֵּס “engineer”.

profile.feeling: The woman engineer — in software, building and industry.

examples.tr: The engineer (f.) is in the office.
There are many women engineers here.

etymology.text: Feminine of מְהַנְדֵּס “engineer” (Wiktionary), from הַנְדָּסָה “engineering”, from Arabic هَنْدَسَة (handasa).

funFacts: The ending ־ֶת marks feminine job nouns of this shape: מְהַנְדֶּסֶת, מוֹכֶרֶת, שׁוֹטֶרֶת.
pitfalls: The ending is ־ֶסֶת (me-han-DE-set), stress on the second-last syllable; plural מְהַנְדְּסוֹת.
subtleties: A mixed team is מְהַנְדְּסִים; מְהַנְדְּסוֹת means women only.

override.N;SG;DEF: Wiktionary gives both נַהָג and נֶהָג as the headword but shows the definite form only for נַהָג (הַנַּהָג); הַנֶּהָג is the definite form of the everyday vocalization נֶהָג used here.
override.N;SG;INDF: Wiktionary gives both נַהָג and נֶהָג as the headword (its declension table follows נַהָג); the course uses the everyday vocalization נֶהָג (nehag) and mentions נַהָג as the normative one.
override.N;PL;DEF: the definite plural of the everyday vocalization נֶהָג (Wiktionary’s table shows only that of נַהָג, הַנַּהָגִים; it lists the indefinite plural נֶהָגִים too).

profile.feeling: Buses, taxis and lorries on Israel’s busy roads.

synonyms.nuance: the normative vocalization of the same word (nahag); Wiktionary gives both, and everyday speech says nehag

etymology.text: From the root נ־ה־ג of נָהַג “to drive; to lead; to behave” (Wiktionary), on the pattern קַטָּל of many professions, like טַבָּח “cook”.

funFacts: The same root gives מִנְהָג “custom” and מַנְהִיג “leader”: a driver, a leader and a custom all “lead”.
pitfalls: With the article the נ doubles: הַנֶּהָג.
Unvowelled נהג is also the verb נָהַג “he drove; he used to”.
subtleties: The feminine is נַהֶגֶת (with patah), plural נַהָגוֹת.

profile.feeling: The woman at the wheel of a bus or a taxi.

examples.tr: My mother is a taxi driver.

etymology.text: Feminine of נַהָג / נֶהָג “driver” (Wiktionary), root נ־ה־ג “to drive, to lead”.

funFacts: Most Israeli job nouns of the pattern קַטָּל make their feminine in ־ֶת: נַהֶגֶת, טַבַּחַת.
pitfalls: The first vowel is a patah (na-HE-get), unlike the masculine נֶהָג; with the article: הַנַּהֶגֶת.
subtleties: Plural נַהָגוֹת (women only).

profile.feeling: The cook in a restaurant, a school or an army kitchen.

examples.tr: He is a cook in a restaurant.
Potiphar, the captain of the guard (“chief of the butchers”)

synonyms.nuance: a chef — the head of a restaurant kitchen, or a celebrated cook

etymology.text: Cognate to Arabic طَبَّاخ (ṭabbāḵ) “a cook” (Wiktionary). The same root gives מִטְבָּח “kitchen” (lesson 12) and טָבַח “to slaughter”.

funFacts: Turkish mutfak “kitchen” comes from Arabic مَطْبَخ (maṭbaḵ) — the same word as Hebrew מִטְבָּח, from the root of טַבָּח.
pitfalls: “To cook” is בִּשֵּׁל (lesson 7) — the verb of this root, טָבַח, means “to slaughter”!
Unvowelled טבח is also טֶבַח “a massacre”.
subtleties: The feminine is טַבַּחַת (Wiktionary); job ads also use the form טַבָּחִית.

profile.feeling: The woman who cooks for a living.

examples.tr: She is a cook in a restaurant.

synonyms.nuance: another feminine form, common in job ads and speech

etymology.text: Feminine of טַבָּח “cook” (Wiktionary), cognate to Arabic طَبَّاخ (ṭabbāḵ).

funFacts: The kitchen she works in, מִטְבָּח, is built from the same root.
pitfalls: The ending ־ַחַת has two patahs: ta-BA-chat; plural טַבָּחוֹת.
subtleties: A female chef is often simply שֶׁפִית or שֶׁף.

profile.feeling: The man behind the counter or at the market stall, calling out his prices.

senses.def: seller (in a sale, as opposed to the buyer)

examples.tr: He is a salesman in a shop.
The seller at the market is nice.

synonyms.nuance: a shop assistant behind the counter

etymology.text: Present participle of מָכַר “to sell”, from the root מ־כ־ר (Wiktionary: the noun follows from the verb).

funFacts: Joseph’s brothers “sold” him with this verb: וַיִּמְכְּרוּ אֶת יוֹסֵף (Genesis 37:28).
pitfalls: It is also the present tense of the verb: הוּא מוֹכֵר פֵּרוֹת “he sells fruit”.
Unvowelled מוכר is also מֻכָּר “familiar, known” (Wiktionary).
subtleties: Many job words are present-tense verb forms used as nouns: מוֹכֵר “selling → seller”, שׁוֹטֵר, פּוֹעֵל.

profile.feeling: The saleswoman at the till or in a clothes shop.

examples.tr: The saleswoman is at the supermarket.
The saleswomen are at the market.

synonyms.nuance: a shop assistant (f.) behind the counter

etymology.text: Feminine of מוֹכֵר, the present participle of מָכַר “to sell” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The feminine present tense of almost every paʿal verb looks like this: מוֹכֶרֶת, אוֹכֶלֶת, שׁוֹטֶרֶת.
pitfalls: Stress on the second-last syllable: mo-CHE-ret; plural מוֹכְרוֹת.
subtleties: It is also the verb: הִיא מוֹכֶרֶת פֵּרוֹת “she sells fruit”.

profile.feeling: Hard hats on a building site; the workers of the labour movement.

synonyms.nuance: an employee — anyone who works, also in an office; פּוֹעֵל is a manual worker

etymology.text: Present participle of פָּעַל “to do, to act, to work”, cognate with Arabic فَعَلَ (faʕala) “to do”, from Proto-Semitic *paʕala (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Hebrew grammar names its verb patterns with this root: פָּעַל, פִּעֵל, הִפְעִיל … and “a verb” is פֹּעַל.
הַפּוֹעֵל “the worker” is the name of many Israeli sports clubs (Wiktionary), founded by the labour movement.
pitfalls: Unvowelled פועל is also פֹּעַל “verb” (the grammar word).
The plural has a hataf patah: פּוֹעֲלִים.
subtleties: פּוֹעֵל is manual work; an office employee is עוֹבֵד.

profile.feeling: The woman on the factory floor or in the fields.

examples.tr: The (women) workers are in the field.

synonyms.nuance: an employee (f.), in any kind of job

etymology.text: Feminine of פּוֹעֵל “worker” (Wiktionary), from פָּעַל “to do, to work”.

funFacts: מוֹעֶצֶת הַפּוֹעֲלוֹת, the Women Workers’ Council of the labour movement (founded in 1921), is the ancestor of today’s women’s organisation נַעֲמַ״ת.
pitfalls: Plural פּוֹעֲלוֹת (women only), with a hataf patah under the ע.
subtleties: It is also the verb form “(she) acts, works”: הַתָּרוּפָה פּוֹעֶלֶת “the medicine works”.

profile.feeling: Fields, orchards and greenhouses of the moshav and the kibbutz.

examples.tr: The farmers are in the field.
The farmer sells fruit at the market.

collocations.tr: a farmer in the moshav (farming village)

synonyms.nuance: a farmer, a peasant — the word of the early Zionist settlers

etymology.text: From חֲקַל “field” (Aramaic) + the suffix ־ַאי (Wiktionary).

funFacts: חֲקַל is the Aramaic “field” of Akeldama, “the field of blood” (Acts 1:19).
The suffix ־ַאי makes other professions too: עִתּוֹנַאי “journalist”.
pitfalls: The plural has a qamats: חַקְלַאי → חַקְלָאִים.
Unvowelled חקלאי is also the adjective חַקְלָאִי “agricultural”.
subtleties: Agriculture is חַקְלָאוּת, from the same word.

profile.feeling: The woman who works her land.

examples.tr: The farmer (f.) is at the market.

etymology.text: Feminine of חַקְלַאי “farmer” (Wiktionary), from Aramaic חֲקַל “field”.

funFacts: The feminine ending ־ִית appears in many job and nationality words: סְטוּדֶנְטִית, אׇמָּנִית, יִשְׂרְאֵלִית.
pitfalls: Unvowelled חקלאית is also the feminine adjective “agricultural”: תּוֹצֶרֶת חַקְלָאִית.
subtleties: Plural חַקְלָאִיּוֹת, with a doubled י.

profile.feeling: Blue uniforms at the square, at the station, at the traffic lights.

examples.tr: The police officer is in the street.
Her father is a police officer.
There are police officers in the square.

phrases.tr: judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself
phrases.meaning: the Biblical command to set up courts and officials

profile.synonymsNone: No neutral synonym; the force is מִשְׁטָרָה “police”.

etymology.text: Believed to have originally meant “scribe” (so translated in the Septuagint); likely ultimately from Akkadian šaṭārum “to write, to inscribe” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Septuagint translated the word “scribe” (Wiktionary): the first שׁוֹטְרִים were officials who wrote.
pitfalls: “The police” is הַמִּשְׁטָרָה; שׁוֹטֵר is one officer.
subtleties: The same root gives שְׁטָר “a document; a banknote” — the old meaning “to write”.

profile.feeling: The policewoman on patrol.

examples.tr: The policewoman is at the station.
The policewoman is standing in the square.

etymology.text: Feminine of שׁוֹטֵר “police officer” (Wiktionary), probably from Akkadian šaṭārum “to write”.

funFacts: Like מוֹכֶרֶת and פּוֹעֶלֶת, it is a feminine present-tense form that became a job noun.
pitfalls: Stress on the second-last syllable: sho-TE-ret; plural שׁוֹטְרוֹת.
subtleties: Before a noun the form stays the same: שׁוֹטֶרֶת־ (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: Contracts, courts and a law office in the city centre.

examples.tr: My lawyer is in the office.

synonyms.nuance: counsel, advocate — formal; the State Attorney’s office is the פְּרַקְלִיטוּת
the written abbreviation, used before a name: עו״ד לֵוִי

etymology.text: עוֹרֵךְ “one who arranges”, present participle of עָרַךְ “to arrange, to draw up”, + דִּין “law, judgement”, cognate with Arabic دِين (dīn) and Aramaic דִּינָא (Wiktionary).

funFacts: פְּרַקְלִיט “counsel” is Greek παράκλητος (“one called to help”), borrowed in Rabbinic times.
pitfalls: The article goes on the second word: עוֹרֵךְ הַדִּין “the lawyer” (the everyday הָעוֹרֵךְ דִּין is not standard).
The plural changes the first word: עוֹרְכֵי דִּין.
subtleties: עוֹרֵךְ alone is an “editor” (of a newspaper, a book or a film).

profile.feeling: The woman lawyer — in court, in a law office, in a contract meeting.

examples.tr: The lawyer (f.) is at the court.

synonyms.nuance: counsel, advocate (f.) — formal

etymology.text: Feminine of עוֹרֵךְ דִּין (Wiktionary): עוֹרֶכֶת “one who arranges” + דִּין “law”.

funFacts: דִּין “law” is the same word as Arabic دِين (dīn), which came to mean “religion”.
pitfalls: “The lawyer (f.)” is עוֹרֶכֶת הַדִּין — the article on the second word.
subtleties: The written abbreviation עו״ד serves for women too.

profile.feeling: Galleries, studios and street art in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem.

examples.tr: The artist is painting in the park.
There are many artists in this city.

synonyms.nuance: a painter — one kind of artist
a craftsman, an artisan; a master of a skill — written the same (אומן) but said uman

etymology.text: Wiktionary gives the origin under the related אֻמָּן “craftsman”: borrowed from Aramaic אוּמָּנָא (ʾūmmānā) “artist, artisan, craftsman”, from Akkadian ummānu “expert, artisan”.

funFacts: Its ancestor, Akkadian ummānu (Wiktionary), was an “expert”: an artist was first of all a master of a craft.
pitfalls: Unvowelled אומן is three words: אׇמָּן “artist” (oman), אֻמָּן “craftsman” (uman) and אוֹמֵן “foster parent” (omen).
The first vowel is a short o (qamats qatan ׇ): o-MAN — not אָמֵן “amen”.
subtleties: Art is אׇמָּנוּת, from the same word.

profile.feeling: The woman artist — a painter, a singer, an actress.

examples.tr: The artist (f.) is in the living room.

synonyms.nuance: a painter (f.)

etymology.text: Feminine of אׇמָּן “artist”, from Aramaic אוּמָּנָא and Akkadian ummānu “expert, artisan” (Wiktionary, under אֻמָּן).

funFacts: The feminine suffix ־ִית is the same as in סְטוּדֶנְטִית and חַקְלָאִית.
pitfalls: Written אומנית in full spelling; the first vowel is a short o: o-ma-NIT.
subtleties: Plural אׇמָּנִיּוֹת with a doubled י.
